title: Daniel Frayne notes the gaps at Muileann òg
summary: A wool-buyer at Tional nan Tuathach's own table tells Daniel Frayne that Fèill Muileann òg now stands with gaps between its tents where none stood before, the fair's own wardens filling them each year with a wider aisle rather than own that the crowd has thinned.

title: The old die broken at Cathair dhearg
summary: With Mairead crowned, the die that struck Eòghan's own likeness on Bonn na Rìoghachd is broken at Cathair dhearg by the mint's custom, the old coin kept good until the new is struck in number enough to answer for it.

title: Daniel Frayne binds primers for Muileann shean
summary: Asked for primers by Muileann shean's own maor, Daniel Frayne binds forty copies of a reading-book at his own bench at Muileann leathan and sends them north on the first cart with room, the forms unchanged since he first set the type twenty years before.

title: Muileann shean's benches pass thirty
summary: The school Muileann shean opened for hewers' children the Guild will not bind grows within the year from eleven pupils to above thirty, though three of the first eleven have already gone south to hire themselves out as chain-hands in the ports.

title: The first bolt off the Doire ghlas looms
summary: The wool mills raised at Doire ghlas with Tional nan Tuathach's own coin turn their first bolt, a grey twill with a white thread at the selvedge, and the overseer writes to Caol mhòr that it is better cloth than the south's own factors reckoned a northern loom could turn out.

title: Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn refuses the first wagon
summary: Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's factors at Àth leathan, the railhead nearest the north, refuse to carry the Doire ghlas mill's first wagon-load south to Muileann òg, giving no reason beyond the Board's own long custom of judging for itself what the line will carry.

title: Tional nan Tuathach brings its suit to Seann Bhral
summary: Daniel Frayne rides west to the circuit court at Seann Bhral with the mill's ledgers and the Board's letter of refusal, asking Ruairidh mac Phàdraig to rule whether a carrier chartered by An Crùn may refuse one people's cargo and take another's.

title: Word of Catrìona nic Neacail's going
summary: A Board clerk's notice of the Mac Ùisdein sale reaches Caol mhòr with a passing word that the surveyor who drew the search's last sheet has resigned her post to teach at Caol shean, a name Daniel Frayne knows only at second hand.

title: The first Doire ghlas bale rides Slighe a' Ghuail
summary: A year after the ruling, Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's own factor at Àth leathan weighs the first Doire ghlas bale onto the wagon without comment, the same weight given any cargo that pays the rate, and Daniel Frayne rides down to see it loaded.

title: Agnes Pike dies
summary: Agnes Pike, who opened the byre school at Doire ghlas in the fifteenth year, dies at seven-and-seventy; Daniel Frayne, reading Muileann shean's letter for primers that season, remembers her telling him that a trade a man carries in his own head weighs nothing on the road.

title: The charter read clause by clause at Seann Bhral
summary: When Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's factor argues at Seann Bhral that the Board's rails answer to a different clause of its charter than its carts, Ruairidh mac Phàdraig has the whole charter read aloud clause by clause, and no clause is found that names the rails apart.

title: The council lets the Board's appeal lapse
summary: Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn's appeal against Breith Seann Bhral lies on the council's table a winter and a spring and is let lapse in the summer, the council's minute noting only that the matter was not reached in the session's business.

title: Mary Coyle dies at Caol mhòr
summary: Mary Coyle, speaker of Tional nan Tuathach from the thirty-third year to the fifty-fifth, dies at Caol mhòr in the second week of an t-Iuchar at nine-and-seventy, having asked that nothing be read over her but the names.

title: Mary Coyle buried near Walter Hale
summary: Mary Coyle is laid in Walter Hale's ground, a little lower on the slope within sight of Tional nan Tuathach's house, and the priest reads over her only the eleven drowned of Cuan bheag, the widows of the bench by the door and her own name; three Ros mhòr men who sailed with her to Seann Bhral bring the tiller of her boat.

title: Mary Coyle's sheet kept in Tional nan Tuathach's chest
summary: Tional nan Tuathach votes without a count that the sheet of the eleven drowned and the widows after them, given it by Mary Coyle's family, be kept in its own chest beside Clàr nan Leòn with the space beneath the last name left empty; no notice of her death goes south.
